title_topic: Airway management in the critically ill
summary: A consultant-level look at the trials that have reshaped peri-intubation care in ICU. INTUBE (JAMA 2021, 2,964 patients, 29 countries) found major adverse peri-intubation events in 45.2% of intubations, mostly cardiovascular instability (42.6%), with cardiac arrest in 3.1%. DEVICE (NEJM 2023) improved first-pass success with videolaryngoscopy (85.1% vs 70.8%) without changing severe complications, though more than 90% of operators were trainees. BOUGIE (JAMA 2021) found no first-pass advantage for bougie over stylet (80.4% vs 83.0%). PREOXI (NEJM 2024) halved peri-intubation hypoxaemia with NIV preoxygenation (9.1% vs 18.5%) without more aspiration, and a 2025 network meta-analysis ranked NIV above HFNO above face mask. In the RSI trial (NEJM, online Dec 2025, 2,365 patients), ketamine did not reduce 28-day mortality compared with etomidate (28.1% vs 29.1%) and caused more cardiovascular collapse (22.1% vs 17.0%), which 2026 network meta-analyses support. PrePARE and PREPARE II found no benefit from a routine 500 mL fluid bolus. Trials of prophylactic vasopressors in ICU have not reported (PREVENTION, NCT05014581, registered as recruiting). The UK critical care guideline is still the 2018 DAS/ICS/FICM/RCoA guideline (BJA, online 2017). DAS published its 2025 guideline for unanticipated difficult intubation in adults, which adds a physiologically difficult airway section and keeps a linear Plan A to D, where the ICU guideline combines Plans B and C. We found no 2025 ICS/DAS critical care update.
takeaways: Use a videolaryngoscope first for ICU intubation: DEVICE showed better first-pass success, mainly with less experienced operators, but no fewer severe complications.
A stylet is a reasonable default: BOUGIE found no first-pass advantage for bougie-first.
Preoxygenate with NIV: PREOXI halved hypoxaemia without increasing aspiration.

Ketamine is not the haemodynamically safer choice: in the RSI trial it caused more cardiovascular collapse than etomidate with no mortality difference. Pick the dose carefully and have a vasopressor ready.
Don't give a routine fluid bolus to prevent collapse: PrePARE and PREPARE II were both negative.
